notes.meaning: King Darius ordered a formal search in the archives of Babylon, where official records and treasures were kept. The Persian officials looked there first to find the original decree made by King Cyrus allowing the Jews to rebuild the temple.

The scroll was not in Babylon, but in the fortress of Ecbatana in the province of Media. This city served as a summer residence for the Persian kings. God guided the search so the old memorandum was preserved and safely recovered.

The memorandum proved that King Cyrus had ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices. Cyrus allowed it to be up to sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide, showing royal permission for a large and sturdy building.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that the Hebrew Bible does not describe the finished building's actual size beyond these permitted dimensions, emphasizing instead that the temple had to stand on the exact site of the first one.

notes.meaning: The decree specified that the structure should have three courses of large stones and one layer of timber. Cyrus had also promised that the building expenses would be paid from the royal treasury.

Cyrus had also commanded that the gold and silver articles taken by King Nebuchadnezzar must be returned. Every sacred item was to be brought back to Jerusalem and placed where it belonged in the house of God.

After confirming the decree, King Darius ordered Tattenai and the other regional officials to stay away from the temple site. Instead of stopping the Jews as their enemies had hoped, the king told the governors not to meddle or interfere.
Darius insisted that the work on the temple must continue without hindrance. He commanded that the Jewish governor and the elders be left alone to rebuild God's house on its original location.

The king ordered that the costs of building be paid to the Jewish elders out of the royal taxes collected in that very province. God turned the officials' challenge into the very means of paying for the construction.

Darius commanded that the priests in Jerusalem be given young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings, along with wheat, salt, wine, and oil. These supplies were needed for the daily grain and animal offerings and had to be provided every day without fail.

Darius wanted the priests to offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. Even though he was a pagan ruler, he respected the God of Israel and valued the prayers of God's people.

A harsh penalty was set for anyone who altered this royal decree. A wooden beam would be pulled from the offender's own house to hang or impale him, and his home would be turned into a pile of rubble.

Darius called on the God who made His Name dwell in Jerusalem to overthrow any king or nation that tried to destroy the temple. The king closed his command by requiring that it be carried out with great speed and care.
Governor Tattenai and his associates obeyed the royal order right away. Because Darius had written so strictly, the local leaders acted quickly to assist the Jews rather than cause more delays.

The Jewish elders made rapid progress because they were encouraged by the preaching of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. They completed the work under the command of God and through the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and later Artaxerxes, who gave gifts to beautify the finished temple.

The temple was completely finished on the third day of the month of Adar, during the sixth year of King Darius's reign. This brought an end to over twenty years of waiting and hardship since the original foundation had been laid.

The priests, the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles celebrated the dedication of the temple with great joy. They set the building apart for holy worship and rejoiced that God's house was standing once again.

For the dedication, the people offered hundreds of bulls, rams, and lambs, as well as twelve male goats for a sin offering—a sacrifice asking God to forgive and remove guilt. Giving twelve goats showed their faith that all twelve tribes still belonged to God as one covenant family.

The leaders organized the priests and Levites into their regular divisions to serve in the temple, just as Moses had written in the law. Now that the building was complete, they made sure that public worship would be held in an orderly, biblical way.

Only a few weeks after finishing the temple, the exiles celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. This feast remembered how God had delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt, which had deep meaning for people newly freed from Babylon.

All the priests and Levites purified themselves together and were ceremonially clean according to the law. Because the Levites were fully prepared, they slaughtered the Passover lambs for all the people and for the priests, allowing the priests to carry out their sacred duties without delay.

The Passover meal was eaten by the returned exiles and by all who had turned away from the impure practices of the surrounding peoples to seek the Lord God of Israel. Taking part in this feast required a true break from idolatry and a genuine commitment to follow God.

The people celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with overflowing joy because the Lord had given them good reason to rejoice. God had changed the heart of the Persian ruler—called the king of Assyria because he ruled that ancient empire's lands—to help them complete the house of God.
